98092356.s: Al Noor Mall is a shopping centre that meets all its visitors' needs for shopping, services and entertainment, drawing well-known local and international brands, with a variety of shops, restaurants and entertainment. It covers more than 90,000 square metres over 3 floors: the first has the main local and international stores, the second is devoted to restaurants, and the third holds the prayer room and restrooms. The mall also has shops selling souvenirs for visitors. It is on King Abdullah Road in Al Uyoun District near the Administrative Court, and is open every day of the week from 10:00 am to 11:00 pm.

98092354.s: Souq Suwaiqa is one of the most important old, historic markets of Madinah. It used to lie west of the Prophet's Mosque, running from Bab Al Salam to Al Ghamama Mosque. The market was destroyed by a huge fire in 1397 AH, and the modern Souq Suwaiqa was then launched to echo the old markets that had vanished, combining modernity with historic heritage. The Governor of Madinah launched the project under the patronage of the Social Development Bank and with the support of Nama Al Munawwara, as part of empowering women in the job market, giving the city's young women opportunities in supplying and selling handmade crafts with a heritage character. The market is in the Heritage District within King Fahd Central Park in the south of the city, and is open Saturday to Thursday from 5 pm to 11 pm.

98092346.s: Souq Al-Tabbakha is a gathering of long-established Madinah restaurants, designed to preserve the traditional spirit and popular life of Madinah, and blending the cultures, flavours and cooking styles of the Islamic world. It has more than 60 outlets competing to serve a variety of popular dishes such as mandi, madhbi, trotters, kebab and fish, along with dishes from across the Islamic world with a Madinah flavour, such as kabuli, bukhari, maqalqal, kammuniya, manto and yaghmash. The market is more than forty years old, and the Madinah Municipality has renovated it fully and in a modern style that echoes Madinah's heritage, making it an important tourist frontage that draws visitors and tourists of many nationalities.

The place has several seating styles, called "Al Waha" (the Oasis), "Al Rawnaq" (Elegance) and "Al Badr" (the Full Moon), each with its own distinct character. The farm is open all year; its hours change in Ramadan (8 pm to 3 am) and on Eid days (5 pm to 9 am). Contact: 0553354486.

98092292.s: Bir Al-Khatim is one of Madinah's most important wells, about 38 metres west of Quba Mosque. It was formerly known as "Bir Aris", after a man called Aris, and became famous as "Bir Al-Khatim" (the Ring Well) after the Prophet's ring (peace be upon him) fell into it. Two famous stories are linked to the well. In the first, the Prophet (peace be upon him) sat on its wall with his legs dangling into it, and Abu Bakr, then Omar, then Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them, came to him in turn and he gave each of them glad tidings of Paradise. In the second, Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, was wearing the Prophet's ring, which the caliphs inherited one after another, and while he was at the well it slipped from his hand into it and could not be found despite searching.

98092290.s: Aliyah Madinah Farms hold a historic social standing: they are farms that the Companion Mukhayriq gave as charity to the Prophet (peace be upon him) before he was killed at the Battle of Uhud, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) distributed them among the Muslims. Mukhayriq had accepted Islam shortly before the battle, gave away his wealth, and fought alongside the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) until he died. The farms are a dense group of connected palm farms, starting from one kilometre from the Prophet's Mosque, with green scenery and areas set up for sitting and strolling among the palms and natural water channels, along with places selling dates, among the finest in the region. The farms are in Al Aliyah District on Ali ibn Abi Talib Road, at the intersection with Prince Abdulmajeed bin Abdulaziz.

98092227.s: Bir Al-Fuqayr carries the story of how Salman the Persian, may Allah be pleased with him, was freed from slavery. In his youth Salman left his homeland, Persia, in search of the true religion, and ended up a slave working in the orchards of a man of Bani Qurayzah in Madinah. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) migrated to Madinah, Salman recognised the signs of prophethood and accepted Islam. The Prophet (peace be upon him) told him to make a contract with his master to buy his freedom, and his master asked for forty ounces of gold and the planting of 300 palm trees in the Al-Fuqayr area until they bore fruit. The Companions rushed to help with saplings, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) told Salman to dig for them, then planted them with his own blessed hands, and they bore fruit that same year. The Prophet (peace be upon him) also gave him gold, which was weighed out to his master as forty ounces, and Salman became free.

98092225.s: Al-Rawha is a broad area on the old caravan route between Madinah and Makkah, stretching about 25 kilometres south-west of Madinah from Sharaf Al-Rawha to Al-Munsaraf (Al-Musayjid). It is rich in historic landmarks, mountains, ravines and valleys, and it is said to have been a route for prophets travelling to the Sacred House for pilgrimage. The Prophet (peace be upon him) prayed in many places there, and its best-known sites include Sharaf Al-Rawha, Irq Al-Zabya, Bir Al-Rawha, Mount Warqan, Mount Shanuka and Fajj Al-Rawha. The Prophet (peace be upon him) took this route to the Battle of Badr, the conquest of Makkah, the Farewell Pilgrimage and other expeditions. The area received great attention in the Saudi era: the well was restored and the surrounding area developed.

98092223.s: Bir Al-Hujaym lies south-west of Al Usbah District, with an ancient mosque beside it to the north, and is about 1,450 metres from Quba Mosque. It is named after a fortified tower that stood near it, and is also called "Al-Hujayr" or "Al-Hujm". Its origin goes back to Bani Majda'a and Bani Jahjaba ibn Kulfa of the Aws, who lived in Al Usbah. The biography books mention that the Prophet (peace be upon him) prayed in the nearby Masjid Al-Tawba in Al Usbah, but nothing indicates that he drank from the well directly. It is a shallow well lined with black lava stone, fed by Wadi Ranuna, and it has been renewed and maintained over the years; people still drink from it and perform ablution there.

98092222.s: Bir Al-Ihn, also known as "Al-Yasira", lies in the homes of Bani Umayyah ibn Zayd al-Awsi of the Ansar, and in pre-Islamic times was called "Al-Abira" or "Al-Asira". It is reported that the Prophet (peace be upon him) visited Bani Umayyah, performed ablution from their well, blessed it and spat into it, and changed its name to "Al-Yasira". It is also mentioned that the Companion Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi was washed with its blessed water when he died. Historians of the eighth and ninth centuries AH described it as a plentiful well in the middle of a lush garden. With time it fell out of use and was abandoned, and the Heritage Commission surrounded it with a wall to protect it, under the project to preserve historic landmarks, ahead of its restoration.

98092201.s: Bir Ghars is a historic landmark linked to the Prophet's biography (peace be upon him). It is in Al Awali District on Qurban Road, south of the Prophet's Mosque, and 1,500 metres north-east of Quba Mosque. It was dug by Malik ibn al-Nahhat, grandfather of Sa'd ibn Khaythama, in whose house the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) stayed when he migrated to Madinah. Many Prophetic reports are attached to the well, including that the Prophet (peace be upon him) drank from it and prayed for it to be blessed, and described it as "a spring from Paradise". Prince Faisal bin Salman bin Abdulaziz launched its restoration and development; it was surrounded by a roofed iron screen and a plaza paved in natural stone, and water is pumped from it again to provide drinking water for visitors. It can be reached from Ali ibn Abi Talib Road, next to the Al Shawi private schools.

It hosts film screenings and interactive workshops in art, science and music, as well as events and performances in collaboration with leading French institutions.

The reserve is known for its towering red rock formations and valleys covered in wildflowers, and offers guided safari tours, hiking trails and stargazing sessions.
